commit.message:
8396147: javac launcher: set -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 for small source sets

Abstract
--------

Most `javac` tool calls are short-lived, and for them the cost of the
default tiered compilation can outweigh what it gives back. This PR
adds a simple heuristic to the `javac` launcher: when the **total size**
of the Java source files to be compiled is below a 2 MiB threshold, the
launcher adds `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1` to the JVM options. On the 375
real-world projects we measured, all 148 projects that trigger the
heuristic (under 2 MiB, compiled with `javac` directly) compile at
least 5% faster, with speedups up to 56%, and no project regresses by
5% or more.

Background
----------

Tiered compilation is costly for short-lived processes and can make up
a large part of their wall time. For example, a build of tablesaw [1]
(398 `.java` files, 1.74 MiB of sources) on an AMD Turin machine, with
different JVM options:
```
| JIT mode                                       | 1 CPU  | 16 CPUs |
|------------------------------------------------|-------:|--------:|
| default (C1 with profiling, then C2)           | 23.41s |   8.33s |
| default, speculative traps disabled (*)        | 23.35s |   8.24s |
| C1 with profiling, no C2 (TieredStopAtLevel=3) | 17.78s |  15.71s |
| C1 only, no profiling (TieredStopAtLevel=1)    | 12.07s |   7.42s |

(*) -XX:PerMethodTrapLimit=0 -XX:PerBytecodeTrapLimit=0
    -XX:PerMethodSpecTrapLimit=0; deoptimizations drop from 593 to 24
    at 1 CPU and from 1686 to 59 at 16 CPUs.
```
We can see that tiered compilation accounts for a large share of the
cost. It first runs slower, profiled code to collect profiles, then
spends CPU time on C2, and this pays off only over a long run. A
short-lived process exits before it does.

`javac` is usually such a process: it compiles a set of sources once
and exits; it is not a long-running service. And while each `javac` run
is short, frequent invocations in scripts, CI pipelines, and automated
workflows (such as AI coding agents working on tasks like SWE-bench [2])
make the cumulative wall-time overhead significant.

How to fix it
-------------

Users expect a fix that works out of the box. The mechanisms that exist
today do not provide one for `javac`:

- The AOT cache of Project Leyden [3] can hold loaded classes, profiles
  and compiled code, but it has to be created by a training run, and the
  JDK does not ship one for `javac` currently.
- The default CDS archive that ships with the JDK contains no `javac`
  classes, and CDS only saves class loading and linking time; it does
  not change JIT compilation.

The key is to reduce the cost of tiered compilation for short-lived
runs. `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1` does that: it compiles hot methods with
C1 only, without profiling, so a method gets its final code at its
first compilation, and C2 is never involved. The JDK build itself
already uses this option (see `JAVA_FLAGS_SMALL` in
`make/autoconf/boot-jdk.m4`). This PR makes the option the default for
`javac` runs that a simple heuristic predicts to be short-lived.

This change
-----------

1. Adds a heuristic in the `javac` launcher: before the JVM is created,
   it sums the sizes of the `.java` source files given on the command
   line and in `@argfiles`. If the total is **below 2 MiB**, it adds
   `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1`; otherwise the JVM options are unchanged.

2. The option is added before the user's options, so
   `-J-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=<level>` on the command line overrides it.
   `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` does not, because the VM applies it before the
   launcher's options.

3. Documents `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=` in the `java` man page and
   documents the automatic heuristic and `-J-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=`
   override under `-J` in the `javac` man page (without exposing the
   internal threshold).

4. New test `test/jdk/tools/launcher/JavacTieredStopHeuristicTest.java`.

Test results
------------

The patch was tested on 375 real projects: 213 from the 10,000 most
popular artifacts on Maven Central, 159 from the 2,000 most-starred
Java repositories on GitHub, and 3 SWE-bench workloads (189 compiled
directly with `javac`, 186 built with Maven). Each was compiled on Arm
Neoverse V2, AMD Turin and NVIDIA Vera machines with 1 to 64 CPUs.
`ratio = patched_wall_time / base_wall_time` is computed on each
machine, and `mean_ratio` is the mean over the three machines; smaller
is better. Median wall time stops improving beyond 4 CPUs, so testing
up to 64 CPUs.
```
| mean_ratio     | 1 CPU | 4 CPUs | 8 CPUs | 32 CPUs | 64 CPUs |
|----------------|------:|-------:|-------:|--------:|--------:|
| <= 0.95        | 39.5% |  39.5% |  39.5% |   39.5% |   40.0% |
| 0.95-1.05      | 60.3% |  60.5% |  60.3% |   60.5% |   59.7% |
| >= 1.05        |  0.3% |   0.0% |  0.3% |    0.0% |    0.3% |
| average        |  0.84 |   0.92 |   0.93 |    0.93 |    0.93 |
```

- Heuristic hit rate: out of the 189 projects compiled directly with
  `javac`, 148 (78.3%, or 39.5% of all 375 projects) are below 2 MiB and
  trigger the heuristic; the remaining 41 `javac` projects are >= 2 MiB,
  and the 186 Maven projects do not trigger it (see Limitation 5).
- 100% of the 148 projects that trigger the heuristic compile 5% or more
  faster at every CPU count: average `mean_ratio` is 0.58 (up to 56%
  faster) at 1 CPU, 0.81 (up to 29% faster) at 4-8 CPUs, and 0.84 (up to
  26% faster) at 32-64 CPUs. The gain is largest with few CPUs, where C2
  competes most with the compiler threads.
- Nearly all of the remaining ~60% (0.95-1.05) did not trigger the
  heuristic (either >= 2 MiB or built by Maven); the single case at 1, 8
  and 64 CPUs with >= 1.05 is also a project the heuristic did not apply
  to, so it is measurement noise.
- The OpenJDK build time is essentially unchanged, as expected: the
  build already compiles with `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1`.

Please see the attachments in JDK-8396147 for detailed test results.

Limitations
-----------

1. It applies only to the `javac` launcher, not to the compiler API
   (`javax.tools`) or any other JDK tool.

2. It does not apply when an option that makes `javac` compile sources
   it cannot count, run plugins, or use an AOT cache is given, on the
   command line or in an `@argfile`:
   ```
     -sourcepath, --source-path,
     --module-source-path, -m, --module,
     --patch-module,
     -processor, -processorpath, --processor-path,
     --processor-module-path,
     -proc:full, -proc:only, -Xprint, -A<key>,
     -Xplugin:<name>,
     -J-XX:AOTCache=<file>, -J-XX:AOTCacheOutput=<file>,
     -J-XX:AOTConfiguration=<file>, -J-XX:AOTMode=<mode>
   ```
   Nor does it apply when `JDK_JAVAC_OPTIONS` is set, when no `.java`
   source is given, or when a `.java` argument cannot be found or read.

3. Any argument that does not start with `-` and ends in `.java` is
   counted, including one that is not a source file. This can only make
   the heuristic more conservative.

4. Sources that `javac` finds on the class path, without `-sourcepath`,
   are not counted.

5. Many real projects are compiled by build tools such as Maven and
   Gradle, which may or may not run the `javac` launcher (for example,
   Maven compiles in-process by default, and tablesaw above runs via
   Maven unless compiled directly). When they do not, the heuristic does
   not apply. The `javac` and `java` man pages document
   `-J-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=<level>` and `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=<level>`,
   so users, and AI agents that drive the build, can apply them where it
   pays.

6. The heuristic and its 2 MiB threshold are derived empirically from
   tests on 189 real projects across current JDKs. As HotSpot evolves
   (for example, lower C2 startup overhead or out-of-the-box Project
   Leyden AOT caching for `javac`), the optimal crossover may shift and
   the fixed 2 MiB threshold may become sub-optimal near the boundary.
   Even so, near the threshold the difference between using
   `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1` or not is small.

7. Because the heuristic lives in `java.base` (`libjli`) and mirrors a
   subset of `javac`'s CLI and `@argfile` syntax, future `javac` options
   that introduce implicit sources or heavy compilation work must be
   kept in sync here; otherwise the heuristic may apply where it should
   have declined.

<details>
<summary> How is this heuristic derived?</summary>
------------------------------

Of the factors we examined, total source size is the main factor in
whether `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1` pays. The JDK version and the machine
shift the size of the gain, but not where it ends.

1. Goal: find when `-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1` (Tier1) gives a shorter
   wall time than the default JVM options, that is, when
   `ratio = tier1_wall_time / default_wall_time < 1.0`.

2. Candidate factors: the `javac` implementation (JDK version), the
   execution environment (machine and CPU count), the total source
   size, the number of files, and the code density (code bytes /
   total bytes).

3. Machines: Arm Neoverse V2 (NVIDIA Grace and AWS Graviton4), AMD
   Turin and NVIDIA Vera, with 1, 4, 8, 32 and 64 CPUs.

4. Test sets:
   - 189 real projects from Maven Central whose published sources can
     be compiled by running `javac` directly. Each was compiled with
     Tier1 always on and with the default options; `mean_ratio` is the
     mean of the three machines' ratios.
   - Generated sources, to vary the total size, the number of files and
     the code density independently of each other.

5. JDK version: on JDK 25 the mean ratio over the 189 projects is 0.02
   (1 CPU) to 0.07 (64 CPUs) higher than on mainline, so Tier1 gains a
   little less. But the smallest project that does not gain,
   `mean_ratio >= 0.995`, is the same 2.25 MiB project on both. The JDK
   version shifts the gain, not the threshold.

6. Execution environment: the mean ratio differs between the three
   machines by up to 0.07, but on each of them the smallest project
   that does not gain is the same 2.25 MiB project.

7. Total source size: with generated sources (JDK 28, 8 CPUs on Grace),
   the median ratio is about 0.74-0.85 below 1 MiB; above 1 MiB, it
   grows with the total size and crosses 1.0 at about 8 MiB.

8. Number of files: with generated sources of the same total size,
   going from 1 file to 20000 files moves the ratio by only 0.016-0.056.

9. Code density: `javac` does less work on whitespace and comments than
   on code, so denser sources cost more. Even so, with generated sources
   of up to about 2.8 MiB, Tier1 pays even at nearly 100% code density.

10. So the total source size is the deciding factor, and the heuristic
    uses only it. The threshold is then chosen from the real-project
    results. Across all tested CPU counts, the smallest project that
    does not benefit from Tier1 is `2.25 MiB`, so the threshold is set
    conservatively at `2 MiB`.
</details>

[1] https://github.com/jtablesaw/tablesaw
[2] https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench
[3] https://openjdk.org/projects/leyden/
